sp24_mt2_MT2.1.title: MT2.1 - Permutation Matrices
sp24_mt2_MT2.1.description: Studies properties of permutation matrices including orthogonality and invariance of statistical properties under permutations.
concepts: Permutation matrices: binary matrices with exactly one 1 per row and column
Mean and variance under linear transformations

problem_statement.definition: P is n×n matrix with: (1) all entries 0 or 1, (2) exactly one 1 per column, (3) exactly one 1 per row
problem_statement.part_c: For y = Px, show: (i) mean(y) = mean(x), (ii) variance(y) = variance(x), (iii) find covariance(x,y)

part_a.key_observation: P^T has exactly one 1 per row (from P's column structure) and one 1 per column (from P's row structure)
part_a.diagonal_entries: For (P^T P)_ii: dot product of i-th row of P^T with i-th column of P
part_a.analysis: i-th row of P^T is i-th column of P, which has exactly one 1 at position k. i-th column of P also has exactly one 1 at the same position k. Therefore (P^T P)_ii = 1
part_a.off_diagonal_entries: For (P^T P)_ij where i≠j: i-th column of P has 1 at position k, j-th column has 1 at position ℓ≠k. Since each row has exactly one 1, positions k and ℓ are different, so dot product is 0
part_a.consequence: P is orthogonal matrix, so P^(-1) = P^T

part_b.interpretation: PAP^T performs a simultaneous row and column permutation of A

part_c_i.key_property: 1^T P = 1^T because P sums each row to 1 (exactly one 1 per row)
part_c_i.proof_1T_P: Each entry of 1^T P is sum of entries in corresponding column of P, which equals 1

part_c_ii.use_P_T_1_equals_1: P^T 1 = 1 (same reasoning: sum of each column of P is 1)
part_c_ii.use_orthogonality: ||Pv||² = (Pv)^T(Pv) = v^T P^T P v = v^T v = ||v||² (since P^T P = I)

part_c_iii.definition: σ_xy = (1/n)⟨x - μ_x 1, y - μ_y 1⟩ = (1/n)x^T y - μ_x μ_y
part_c_iii.use_means_equal: μ_y = μ_x, so σ_xy = (1/n)x^T Px - μ²_x
part_c_iii.alternative_form: Using variance: σ²_x = (1/n)x^T x - μ²_x, so (1/n)x^T x = σ²_x + μ²_x
part_c_iii.answer: σ_xy = (1/n)x^T Px - μ²_x or equivalently σ_xy = σ²_x (when P=I, covariance equals variance)

formulas: Permutation matrix: exactly one 1 per row and column

sp24_mt2_MT2.2.title: MT2.2 - Correlation Coefficient
sp24_mt2_MT2.2.description: Analyzes correlation coefficient for 2-vectors, showing it must be ±1 and relating it to affine relationships.

problem_statement.given: x, y ∈ ℝ² with x₁ ≠ x₂ and y₁ ≠ y₂
problem_statement.part_b: For y = βx + γ1, show: (i) β ≠ 0, (ii) γ = μ_y - βμ_x, (iii) ρ_xy = -1 if β<0, +1 if β>0
problem_statement.part_c: True or False: any x,y in ℝ² can be expressed as affine functions of each other

part_a.dimension_argument: In ℝ², any two nonzero vectors are either parallel or span the entire space
part_a.key_insight: x̃ and ỹ are both nonzero (since x₁≠x₂ and y₁≠y₂) and both lie in ℝ²
part_a.conclusion: Both x̃ and ỹ are parallel to [1,-1]^T in ℝ²
part_a.correlation: Since x̃ = α[1,-1]^T and ỹ = β[1,-1]^T where α = (x₁-x₂)/2 and β = (y₁-y₂)/2

part_b_i.then: y = γ1 means y₁ = y₂ = γ (all components equal)

part_b_ii.de_mean: ỹ = y - μ_y 1 = βx + (μ_y-βμ_x)1 - μ_y 1 = βx - βμ_x 1 = β(x - μ_x 1) = βx̃

part_b_iii.answer: ρ_xy = -1 if β < 0, and ρ_xy = +1 if β > 0

part_c.statement: True or False: Any x,y ∈ ℝ² with x₁≠x₂ and y₁≠y₂ can be expressed as affine functions of each other
part_c.explanation: From part (a), we showed ρ_xy = ±1, meaning x̃ and ỹ are parallel (linearly dependent)
part_c.details: Since ỹ = λx̃ for some λ ≠ 0, we have: y - μ_y 1 = λ(x - μ_x 1)
part_c.so_y_of_x: y = βx + γ1 where β = λ and γ = μ_y - λμ_x
part_c.so_x_of_y: x = β'y + γ'1 where β' = 1/λ and γ' = μ_x - μ_y/λ
part_c.conclusion: Yes, any such pair can be expressed as affine functions of each other

formulas: Correlation: ρ_xy = ⟨x̃,ỹ⟩/(||x̃||||ỹ||) where x̃ = x - μ_x 1
Sign function: sgn(α) = α/|α| = +1 if α>0, -1 if α<0
Linear dependence in ℝ²: any two nonzero vectors are parallel
Cauchy-Schwarz: |⟨x,y⟩| ≤ ||x||||y|| with equality iff x,y parallel

sp24_mt2_MT2.3.title: MT2.3 - Gram-Schmidt Algorithm and Solving Ax=b
sp24_mt2_MT2.3.description: Applies Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to three vectors in ℝ³ and uses the result to solve a linear system.
concepts: Solving Ax = b using QR factorization

problem_statement.part_a: Apply Gram-Schmidt to get q₁, q₂, q₃ orthonormal with span(a₁,...,aₖ) = span(q₁,...,qₖ)
problem_statement.part_b: Solve Ax = b where A = [a₁ a₂ a₃] and b = [1, √2, √2]^T

part_b.setup: A = QR where Q = [q₁ q₂ q₃] is orthogonal
part_b.compute_R: R = Q^T A (using orthogonality Q^T Q = I)

solve_Ax_equals_b.multiply_by_QT: Rx = Q^T b (using Q^T Q = I)

formulas: Gram-Schmidt: vₖ = aₖ - Σᵢ₌₁^(k-1) ⟨aₖ,qᵢ⟩qᵢ, then qₖ = vₖ/||vₖ||
QR decomposition: A = QR where Q^T Q = I and R upper-triangular
R entries: rᵢⱼ = ⟨qᵢ,aⱼ⟩ for i ≤ j
Solving Ax = b: Rx = Q^T b (then back-substitution)

sp24_mt2_MT2.4.title: MT2.4 - Projection Matrices
sp24_mt2_MT2.4.description: Studies projection matrix P = aa^T/(a^T a) that projects vectors onto span(a), exploring its properties and the complementary projection S = I - P.

problem_statement.setup: a,b ∈ ℝⁿ nonzero, b ∉ span(a), find b̂ = αa ∈ span(a) closest to b
problem_statement.part_a: Show P = aa^T/(a^T a) where b̂ = Pb
problem_statement.part_c: Show: (i) P^T = P, (ii) P^k = P for all k≥1 with geometric interpretation
problem_statement.part_e: For S = I - P: (i) Find S^k, (ii) If Py=0 find Sy, (iii) Show {a} is basis for N(S), (iv) Find rank(S)

part_a.orthogonality_condition: ε = b - b̂ must be orthogonal to a: ⟨a, b-b̂⟩ = 0
part_a.express_bhat: b̂ = αa = (a^T b)/(a^T a) · a = [aa^T/(a^T a)]b
part_a.answer: P = aa^T/(a^T a) where a^T a is scalar and aa^T is n×n matrix

part_b.reasoning: aa^T has all columns proportional to a (each column is (a_j)a where a_j is component of a)
part_b.alternative: P maps ℝⁿ onto span(a) which is 1-dimensional, so rank = 1

part_c_i.compute_transpose: P^T = [aa^T/(a^T a)]^T = (aa^T)^T/(a^T a) = (a^T)^T a^T/(a^T a) = aa^T/(a^T a) = P

part_c_ii.simplify: P² = a(a^T a)a^T/(a^T a)² = aa^T/(a^T a) = P
part_c_ii.induction: By induction: P^k = P·P^(k-1) = P·P = P² = P for all k ≥ 1
part_c_ii.geometric_interpretation: P projects onto span(a). Projecting twice (or k times) is same as projecting once, because once a vector is in span(a), projecting it again doesn't change it.

part_d.since_a_nonzero: a ≠ 0, so must have (a^T y)/(a^T a) = 0
part_d.interpretation: y is orthogonal to a. Geometric meaning: if projection of y onto span(a) is zero, then y must be perpendicular to a.

part_e_i.use_P2_equals_P: S² = I - 2P + P = I - P = S
part_e_i.induction: S^k = S·S^(k-1) = S·S = S² = S for all k ≥ 2
part_e_i.answer: S^k = S for all k ≥ 1 (S is idempotent)

part_e_ii.interpretation: If y is in nullspace of P (i.e., perpendicular to a), then S acts as identity on y. This makes sense: P projects onto span(a), S projects onto orthogonal complement of span(a).

part_e_iii.check_a_in_NS: Sa = (I-P)a = a - Pa = a - [aa^T/(a^T a)]a = a - a(a^T a)/(a^T a) = a - a = 0 ✓
part_e_iii.meaning: v equals its projection onto span(a), so v ∈ span(a)
part_e_iii.therefore: v = αa for some scalar α
part_e_iii.conclusion: N(S) ⊆ span{a}. Combined with a ∈ N(S), we have N(S) = span{a}
part_e_iii.basis: Since a ≠ 0, {a} forms a basis for N(S)

part_e_iv.geometric_explanation: S projects onto (n-1)-dimensional orthogonal complement of span(a)

formulas: Idempotent: P² = P (projecting twice = projecting once)
Orthogonal complement projection: S = I - P

sp24_mt2_MT2.5.title: MT2.5 - Inner Products with Matrices
sp24_mt2_MT2.5.description: Explores conditions on matrix W for ⟨x,y⟩_W = x^T Wy to be a valid inner product, including symmetry, positive-definiteness, and invertibility.

problem_statement.part_a: Find W such that ⟨x,y⟩_W = x^T y (Euclidean inner product)
problem_statement.part_b: Show W=[[0,3],[1,0]] is not inner product
problem_statement.part_d: Show if any diagonal entry of W is 0, then not inner product
problem_statement.part_e: Show if W not invertible, then not inner product

part_a.requirement: x^T Wy = x^T y for all x,y
part_a.observe: x^T Iy = x^T y where I is identity matrix

property_1_fails.note: ⟨y,x⟩_W = y^T Wx = (x^T W^T y)^T = x^T W^T y
property_1_fails.comparison: Need x^T Wy = x^T W^T y for all x,y, which requires W = W^T

part_b.answer: Not inner product because W is not symmetric

part_c.property_1: ⟨x,y⟩_W = x^T Wy = x^T W^T y = (Wx)^T y = ⟨Wx,y⟩ = ⟨y,x⟩_W ✓ (when W symmetric)
part_c.properties_2_3: Bilinearity follows from matrix multiplication properties ✓

property_4.recompute: Let's use completing the square properly
property_4.zero_iff: (a-b)² = 0 and (a+b)² = 0 ⟺ a=b and a=-b ⟺ a=b=0 ⟺ z=0

part_c.answer: W = [[2,1],[1,2]] defines a valid inner product ✓

part_d.evaluate: e₁^T We₁ = (first row of W)·e₁ = w₁₁ = 0
part_d.answer: If any diagonal entry is 0, cannot be inner product

part_e.consequence: dim(N(W)) ≥ 1, so ∃ nonzero v with Wv = 0
part_e.answer: If W not invertible, cannot be inner product
part_e.note: This implies W must be invertible (and hence full rank) for ⟨·,·⟩_W to be inner product

formulas: Inner product axioms: (1) symmetry, (2) additivity, (3) homogeneity, (4) positive-definiteness
Quadratic form: x^T Wx = Σᵢⱼ wᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ
Invertibility: W invertible ⟺ N(W) = {0} ⟺ Wv = 0 implies v = 0
